blocks.text: The tips of the tongue are λεπτὰ ὥσπερ τρίχες [lepta hōsper triches] ^{f)}, as thin as hairs. With an eye to this David says, Psal. CXL, 3. They have sharpened their tongues like serpents. Plautus more than once calls them bilingues [two-tongued]. Thus in the Persa: Like a creeping beast, he is two-tongued and wicked. And in the Asinaria Libanus invites Philenium to a kiss thus: Be a creeping beast, so that I may have a double tongue. That is, if we believe Salmasius, serpents flicker their tongue with so tremulous a motion that it seems not single but double. In the same way those who brandished and shook a sarissa were said sarissam duplicare [to double the sarissa], as though by shaking it they made it double. Hence Hesychius: Πτύσσει· κραδαίνει, τὰ δόρατα διπλοῖ [Ptyssei; kradainei, ta dorata diploi], that is, he brandishes the spears and doubles them. And in the Apology of Apuleius, Laelius calls ἴϋγγας [iyngas] inlices bicodulas [two-tailed lures], because by the constant vibration of the tail they make it in some measure double, and so seem to have two tails. From this motion of the tail the Iynx is called σεισοπυγὶς [seisopygis], and motacilla [wagtail]. That some of the ancients held this very opinion is shown by these words of Isidore on the serpent, Orig. book 12, ch. 4: No animal moves its tongue with such speed, so much so that it seems to have a triple tongue, though it has only one. But these things, however plausible, are by no means true. For the serpent is not called bilinguis by Plautus because of the swift vibration of its tongue, but because it has a forked one, as he himself testifies in the Poenulus: With forked tongue, like a creeping beast. Accordingly the Philosopher asserts, in the place cited above, δικρόαν αὐτῶν εἶναι τὴν γλῶτταν ἄκραν [dikroan autōn einai tēn glōttan akran], that the tip of their tongue is cleft. Hence the Arabs in Damir, in the chapter الحية [al-ḥayya], or On the serpent: لسانها مشقوق ولذلك يظن بعض الناس ان لها لسانين [lisānuhā mashqūq wa-li-dhālika yaẓunnu baʿḍ al-nās anna lahā lisānayn] Its tongue is divided; for this reason some think it has two tongues. And in the chapter الضب [al-ḍabb], or On the land crocodile: ولما سال الامام ابو حنيفة عن ذكر الضب فقال انه كلسان الحية اصل واحد له فرعان [wa-lammā saʾala al-imām Abū Ḥanīfa ʿan dhakar al-ḍabb fa-qāla innahu ka-lisān al-ḥayya aṣl wāḥid lahu farʿān] And when the priest Abuchanipha had inquired about the penis of the land crocodile, he said that it is like the tongue of the serpent, which has one root but is forked. Others assert that it is three-forked. Thus Pliny ^{g)}: The tongue of serpents is very thin, and three-forked. The poets generally follow this. Virgil, Georg. book 3 and Aen. book 2:
[III, 243] Towering toward the Sun, it flickers in its mouth with three-forked tongues.
Ovid, on the dragon slain by Cadmus, Metam. book 3:
— — — its whole body swells with poison, and three tongues flicker.
And on the dragon in Colchis, guardian of the golden fleece, Metam. book 7:
Who, conspicuous for his crest and his three tongues.
Here the savage serpent drags its immense body, and thrusts out its three-cleft tongue.
— — — the tongue, brandished through the air with three-cleft motion, flickers, and leaping up licks the sky.
— — and now, now with the tip of its three-forked tongue it was licking the back of the steed wearied by the struggle.
Statius on the Python, book 1 of the Thebaid, line 565:
— — while, stretched out, it gapes with three-forked mouth at the Castalian springs.
And on the serpent by which Archemorus was slain, book 5, line 580:
— the spear flies quivering, and enters the gaping jaws of the monster, and cuts the fierce bonds of the three-forked tongue.

Should we refer to this the fact that the slanderer, who thrusts out his tongue against anyone and flickers it in the manner of a serpent, is assigned a triple tongue in the Chaldee paraphrase, Iob. XXXVI, 33. Ps. CI, 5. and CXL, 12. Eccles. X, 11. etc.? It certainly seems so. Nor do I interpret otherwise these words of Sirach XXVIII, 15. Γλῶσσα τρίτη πολλοὺς ἐσάλευσεν [Glōssa tritē pollous esaleusen], and verse 17, Γλῶσσα τρίτη γυναῖκας ἀνδρείας ἐξέβαλε [Glōssa tritē gynaikas andreias exebale]. Others explain them differently, as we shall observe below.
But this interpretation is strongly confirmed by the words of the Psalmist, in which the slanderer's tongue is compared with the tongue of a serpent.
